label: Functions on Varieties
notes: Open the chapter. With varieties defined, we ask what the maps between them are. The deck follows printed pages 73 through 84 and develops regular functions, polynomial maps, the coordinate ring as a complete invariant, and the equivalence between the geometry of affine varieties and the algebra of finitely generated reduced rings.

label: Regular Functions
notes: Define regular functions on an affine variety as restrictions of polynomials. Two polynomials give the same function exactly when they differ by something vanishing on the variety, so the ring of regular functions is the coordinate ring, the polynomial ring modulo the ideal of the variety. This ring captures all polynomial data on the space.

label: Polynomial Maps
notes: Introduce morphisms of affine varieties: maps given in each coordinate by a polynomial. A morphism between varieties pulls regular functions back to regular functions, inducing a ring homomorphism between coordinate rings in the opposite direction. This contravariance is the algebraic signature of a genuinely geometric map.

label: The Coordinate Ring as Invariant
notes: Show that the coordinate ring determines the variety. A morphism corresponds precisely to a homomorphism of coordinate rings, and an isomorphism of varieties matches an isomorphism of rings. Thus the coordinate ring is a complete invariant: everything about an affine variety is encoded in this single algebraic object.

label: The Equivalence of Categories
notes: State the punchline. The category of affine varieties is equivalent, contravariantly, to the category of finitely generated reduced algebras over the field. Geometry and algebra are not merely analogous here; they are the same theory viewed from two sides, which lets us move freely between pictures and computations.

label: Recap
notes: Close the chapter. Regular functions form the coordinate ring, morphisms of varieties correspond to homomorphisms of coordinate rings in the opposite direction, and this gives an equivalence between affine varieties and finitely generated reduced algebras. With morphisms in hand, Part III turns to projective and birational geometry.
